entries.name: Flow matching
entries.definition: A generative-model training method that fits a time-dependent vector field by regression to velocities associated with a chosen probability path between a base distribution and a data distribution, with conditional flow matching providing a tractable training objective.
entries.identity_notes: The 442 pinned AIO identities and 90 preceding native identities, including scoped synonyms and aliases, were compared alongside ignored-inclusive searches of both checkouts. This record denotes the general probability-path training method of Lipman and colleagues. Conditional flow matching is its tractable objective construction, not an asserted synonym for every use of the general method. Straight conditional paths overlap with the training construction used in rectified flow; that overlap does not make the general path family and the rectification/reflow procedure identical.
entries.mechanism: The method regresses a neural vector field on a target velocity under a prescribed time-indexed density. Conditional flow matching samples a data-conditioned path and its known conditional velocity; under the paper's assumptions its loss has the same parameter gradient as the marginal flow-matching loss. For the illustrated Gaussian conditional paths, the mean and standard deviation define an affine transformation of base noise. Training avoids integrating the learned ODE, while generation integrates that vector field from the base distribution.
entries.locator: Sections 3–3.2, equations (5)–(9) and Theorems 1–2, PDF pp. 3–4; Section 4, equations (10)–(24), PDF pp. 4–6
entries.title: Flow Matching for Generative Modeling
entries.mapping_rationale: Flow matching uses regression of time- and state-dependent velocity targets. RegressionAnalysis describes the corresponding statistical estimation task, whereas this local concept denotes a generative training algorithm; the mapping does not assert an algorithm is a task.
limitations: The equality of conditional and marginal objective gradients is conditional on the paper's density and integrability assumptions, including positive path density in Theorem 2; finite neural training does not guarantee the ideal field.
The Gaussian construction with positive terminal noise leaves a smoothed approximation to the data distribution. Training without ODE simulation does not remove numerical ODE solving from sampling.
The optimal-transport conditional Gaussian path in Section 4 does not imply that the resulting marginal flow is a globally optimal transport map, as the paper explicitly notes on PDF p. 6.
No benchmark superiority, universal sampling-step count or independently checked theorem proof is asserted.
entries.abstract_interpretation: Introduces a regression-based way to train continuous generative flows with selectable conditional probability paths. Claimed speed or sample-quality advantages were not generalized into record claims.

entries.name: Rectified flow
entries.definition: A transport-learning method that regresses a velocity field on endpoint differences along straight interpolations of coupled samples and uses the resulting ordinary differential equation to transport the source distribution, optionally repeating rectification using the learned endpoint coupling.
entries.identity_notes: The ignored-inclusive identity search covered both checkouts, all 442 AIO labels and scoped synonyms, and 90 preceding native identities. This record denotes the straight-interpolation regression and rectification procedure of Liu, Gong and Liu, including optional reflow. It overlaps with particular conditional flow-matching objectives, but does not denote every probability-path choice in flow matching, a particular trained image generator, or mandatory distillation.
entries.mechanism: Given coupled endpoints X0 and X1, training samples t and regresses v((1−t)X0+tX1,t) toward X1−X0 using squared error. The ideal minimizer is the conditional mean endpoint difference at the interpolated state. Integrating dZt/dt=v(Zt,t) from the source sample induces a new endpoint coupling. Reflow optionally trains another rectified flow on that coupling; endpoint-map distillation is a separate optional step.
entries.locator: Sections 2.1–2.2, equations (1)–(2), Algorithm 1 and transport-cost discussion, PDF pp. 4–6
entries.title: Flow Straight and Fast: Learning to Generate and Transfer Data with Rectified Flow
entries.mapping_rationale: The defining velocity-learning objective estimates conditional endpoint differences by least-squares regression. RegressionAnalysis is the related estimation task, while rectified flow is the transport-learning algorithm and may include iterative reflow; no task/algorithm subclass assertion is made.
limitations: Marginal preservation and transport-cost statements concern ideal regression with a well-posed ODE, not arbitrary finite neural estimates or numerical solvers.
Straight training interpolations do not make the learned marginal trajectories exactly straight; one-step accuracy is not universal. Reflow and distillation are optional.

The original paper explicitly does not guarantee a globally cost-optimal coupling in general. Later analysis also gives nonoptimal zero-loss fixed points for a gradient-constrained rectification variant when required support or regularity assumptions are absent.

The later optimal-transport counterexamples limit stronger equivalence claims; they do not refute the original least-squares construction. No executable solver, numerical benchmark or full proof verification is supplied.

additional_evidence.locator: Sections 3.1–3.2, PDF pp. 5–6; Section 4.1, Proposition 10, Theorem 11 and Remark 12, PDF pp. 7–8
additional_evidence.claim: A later analysis of gradient-constrained rectification exhibits nonoptimal zero-loss fixed points with disconnected intermediate supports; its corrected equivalence theorem additionally requires full intermediate support, rectifiability and smooth potential fields. Straightness or imposing a potential alone does not establish globally optimal transport.

entries.name: Consistency model
entries.definition: A generative model family that learns a noise- or time-conditioned function mapping points on a probability-flow ODE trajectory to its common low-noise endpoint, enabling a sample to be obtained with one model evaluation and allowing optional multistep refinement.
entries.identity_notes: All 442 pinned AIO labels and scoped synonyms and 90 preceding native identities were checked, with ignored-inclusive text searches of both checkouts. The identity is the endpoint-map model family introduced by Song and colleagues, not generic logical consistency, a trained checkpoint, or one particular training loss. Original consistency distillation, original consistency training and improved consistency training are procedures for learning this family and are not aliases for the model family itself.
entries.mechanism: A consistency function assigns the same low-noise endpoint to states on the same probability-flow trajectory. The paper's skip-connected parameterization combines an input skip term and a learned term whose coefficients enforce the identity boundary at the minimum noise level. Generation applies the model to high-noise input; multistep generation interleaves model evaluation with noise injection. The original paper describes both diffusion-model-assisted distillation and direct consistency training with shared-noise adjacent perturbations of a data sample.
entries.locator: Section 3, equation (5), Algorithm 1 and boundary-condition discussion, PDF pp. 3–4; Sections 4–5, Algorithms 2–3, PDF pp. 4–6
entries.title: Consistency Models
entries.mapping_rationale: The consistency-model family is a specific learned representation of a generative distribution/endpoint transformation, within the broader scope of AIO Model. The mapping does not assert equivalence to a distillation procedure or to an adversarial network.
limitations: The learned consistency model is not required to be invertible. Ideal probability-flow properties do not establish exact data recovery or perfect self-consistency for a finite trained model.

The original direct consistency-training teacher uses EMA; the later inspected correction identifies a failure of its original asymptotic justification when teacher and student parameters differ. This record does not endorse that original training argument as generally valid.
The correction concerns consistency training and does not remove EMA from all distillation procedures or from the separate inference-time averaged model.
One-evaluation generation is an available procedure, not a universal image-quality guarantee. No benchmark reproduction or independently verified convergence proof is claimed.

entries.name: Improved consistency training
entries.definition: The consistency-model training procedure of Song and Dhariwal that learns directly from paired shared-noise data perturbations using a stop-gradient teacher with current student parameters, a Pseudo-Huber discrepancy, revised noise weighting and sampling, and a staged increase in noise-discretization intervals.
entries.identity_notes: The identity search included 442 AIO records, 90 preceding native identities, all scoped synonyms and aliases, and ignored-inclusive text in both checkouts. This is the named improved consistency-training procedure, not the consistency-model family, the original EMA-teacher training procedure, diffusion-model distillation, or a particular iCT-deep architecture/checkpoint. The acronym is qualified to avoid claiming an unscoped abbreviation.
entries.mechanism: The student and stop-gradient teacher evaluate the same data sample plus the same Gaussian noise scaled to adjacent noise levels, with teacher EMA decay set to zero. The revised objective uses a Pseudo-Huber discrepancy and inverse adjacent-noise-gap weighting. Training samples adjacent intervals according to discretized lognormal masses and doubles the interval count at scheduled milestones up to a cap. Noise-embedding sensitivity and shared dropout randomness are additional prescribed training choices; the separate inference-time EMA remains distinct.
entries.locator: Section 2, equations (3)–(5), PDF p. 3; Table 1 and Sections 3.1–3.5, equations (6)–(10), PDF pp. 4–8
entries.title: Improved Techniques for Training Consistency Models
entries.mapping_rationale: The procedure is directly related to choosing how a model is trained. The pinned TrainingStrategy definition calls its subject a preprocessing, whereas iCT is the actual optimization/training procedure; related_match preserves this scope discrepancy instead of asserting an unqualified subclass relation. Distillation is not an equivalent target because this procedure learns directly from data without a separately pretrained diffusion teacher.
limitations: Removing teacher EMA retains stop-gradient and does not remove inference-time parameter averaging; it is not a blanket recommendation to eliminate EMA from consistency distillation.
The paper's counterexample diagnoses a flaw in an earlier asymptotic argument. Its correction and finite-noise curriculum do not establish universal finite-training convergence.

Noise distribution, loss scale, discretization cap, dropout and embedding settings are choices evaluated in particular image-generation settings, not universal hyperparameters. The interval count doubles; the number of noise grid points is that count plus one.
The record describes the inspected training procedure and retains DRAFT status; it does not reproduce performance comparisons, certify every proof, or identify all future variants with this version.
entries.abstract_interpretation: Reassesses direct consistency training and proposes revised teacher updates, losses and noise schedules. Full-method reading separates teacher EMA from inference EMA and interval doubling from grid-point count.

source_caveats.observation: The correction addresses a flaw in the earlier asymptotic training justification, not the endpoint-map family identity. Teacher EMA removal is distinct from retained inference EMA. The discretization curriculum doubles the interval count and adds one grid point.

The inspected counterexample and corrected theorem concern stronger optimal-transport claims for a potential-constrained variant. They are not falsely attributed as a refutation of the original unconstrained regression construction.

Equations and multicolumn reading order were checked on the listed rendered pages. No performance-table values are curated. Appendix proofs and executable implementations were not independently certified.

limitations: All four records remain DRAFT and receive adversarial self-review, not independent scientific approval.
Follow-up web-query exact timestamps were not retained; the ledger records the actual known time bound rather than inventing exact times. PDF access timestamps and hashes are exact.
